name: acceptor-connector
intent: Separate passive acceptance and active connection establishment from per-connection handler activation and message processing, so transport setup, protocol negotiation, connection topology and concurrency policy can change without rewriting service logic.
problem: Services often bind/listen/accept or resolve/dial, perform handshakes, select a handler and process messages in one control path. That coupling duplicates setup across ports and protocols, makes accept/connect work block message processing, and turns transport or concurrency-policy changes into service-code edits.
context: Connection-oriented communication software—servers hosting several services and clients dialing them—where setup varies across sockets, TLS, IPC or negotiated protocols, and where a dispatcher (Reactor, Proactor, leader/followers or a pool) must be selectable independently of handler logic. The separation matters most when setup can be expensive, connections are long-lived, or connection storms require admission control.
benefits: Service handlers and the transport/concurrency policy evolve independently: connection-establishment code is written once and reused across services, ports and protocols.
New service types plug in through a handler factory or registry instead of edits to the accept path.
Portability: the same handler is reachable over different transports and can be driven by a Reactor, a Proactor or a thread pool.
Initialisation and failure handling are centralised at connection time (admission checks, resource setup, connection policies).
Protects the passive (listening) endpoint from accidental I/O: only the acceptor/connector touches it; handlers own only the connected endpoint.
tradeoffs: More moving parts than an inline accept loop: acceptor, connector, handler factory and dispatcher must be designed and wired.
For a single service on a single port the indirection often costs more than it saves.
Asynchronous establishment requires dispatcher integration; handler lifetime, registration and cancellation are subtle.
Dynamic dispatch and per-connection handler allocation add setup-time overhead (negligible for long-lived connections, visible for very short ones).
Debugging spans more components: a fault may originate in the transport, the factory or the activation hook.
The acceptor can become a bottleneck under connection storms if the handler factory is expensive; pre-spawning or batching initialisation is required at scale.
Thundering-herd behaviour on listener wakeup is possible with naive select/epoll acceptance; use EPOLLEXCLUSIVE or accept4() with a lock to mitigate.

participants.responsibility: Passively waits for connection requests on a bound endpoint, creates the service handler via the factory, hands the connected endpoint to it and activates it.
Actively initiates a connection to a remote acceptor (optionally through the dispatcher), then creates and activates the service handler for the connected endpoint.
Application-specific endpoint abstraction that exchanges data over the established connection; after activation it is unaware of how the connection was established.
Decides which concrete handler serves a connection (registry lookup by service id) and instantiates it.
Demultiplexes events and completes asynchronous establishment (accept readiness, connect completion), decoupling the roles from the concurrency mechanism (Reactor, Proactor, thread pool).

use_cases: Multi-service network servers that share an endpoint or acceptor boundary (HTTP, logging, remote login and file-transfer services).
Object request brokers and middleware where a service id is resolved at connection time and mapped to a handler factory.
Clients that dial a service and reuse handler code across plain TCP, TLS or IPC transports.
Event-driven servers where accept readiness and connect completion are dispatched by a Reactor, Proactor or leader/followers policy.
Long-lived connections where authentication, protocol negotiation, session state and resource allocation must finish before message processing begins.
Java NIO servers that register ServerSocketChannel for OP_ACCEPT, accept SocketChannel instances and hand them to per-connection handlers.
Netty ServerBootstrap deployments where a parent (boss) EventLoopGroup accepts channels and a child group runs the configured pipeline.
Apache Kafka SocketServer, where an Acceptor accepts per-listener connections, assigns them to Processor selectors and applies bounded connection/request capacity.
Apache Pekko Streams TCP servers, where Tcp(system).bind emits IncomingConnection values and outgoingConnection provides the connector-side flow for each connection.
Connection-oriented protocol gateways that negotiate TLS, ALPN or an application protocol once, then activate a handler selected by the negotiated service identity.
avoid_when: A throwaway script or tool has one socket and one handler: an inline accept loop or standard-library server call is simpler.
The protocol is datagram-based or otherwise connectionless, so there is no establishment phase to decouple.
A framework already internalises the split (Netty, Kestrel, tokio/hyper, asyncio, Go net/http or ASP.NET Core) and exposes handler registration; rebuilding the roles adds accidental complexity.
Connections are terminated by a load balancer or service-mesh sidecar, so this component owns no establishment logic.
Per-connection setup is trivial, traffic is low and no alternate transport, handler registry or dispatcher policy is expected.
Expected concurrency is tiny and the service will not need independent admission control, protocol negotiation or a replaceable connection policy.
anti_patterns: Treating Reactor or Proactor as a replacement for Acceptor-Connector: dispatching readiness or completion events does not by itself separate connection establishment and handler activation from service processing.
One global handler instance shared across connections, with per-connection state smuggled in through globals or thread-local storage.
Thread-per-connection acceptance without a bound, presented as scalability — under load this exhausts memory and context-switch budget.
Re-implementing the acceptor/connector roles on top of a framework that already provides them (Netty, Kestrel, tokio, asyncio, Go net/http).
Permitting unlimited backlog on listen() without admission control; the kernel will buffer connections but application resources are still bounded.

Running blocking TLS certificate loading or private-key operations on an async runtime worker thread: this blocks the entire task and starves other tasks scheduled on that worker. Fix: use tokio::task::spawn_blocking for blocking crypto, or use an async-native-tls library designed for the runtime.

Unbounded connection accumulation with no admission control: accepting connections faster than handlers can initialise or than the downstream service can process requests causes memory growth and eventual OOM. Fix: a bounded semaphore on concurrent handshakes and a connection count cap in the factory.

Closing the listener socket before existing connected handlers have drained: causes clients to receive RST during in-flight requests, leading to retry storms and failed requests. Fix: implement a two-phase shutdown — stop accepting, drain existing handlers, then close.

Missing EPOLLEXCLUSIVE on a multi-acceptor shared listen socket (Linux): multiple epoll-waiting threads can wake for one incoming connection, causing a thundering-herd storm where all call accept() and all but one fail. Fix: use EPOLLEXCLUSIVE, serialize accept() with a lock, or use separate SO_REUSEPORT listening sockets.

Handler outliving the acceptor's reference to it or vice versa: if the acceptor holds a Arc<Handler> and the handler holds an Arc<Acceptor>, neither is ever dropped — memory leak. Fix: use weak references (Arc::downgrade) or ensure the acceptor's reference is dropped after hand-off.

TLS ALPN/protocol negotiation that determines the service handler occurring after the first read: some TLS libraries do not expose ALPN result until after the handshake completes, forcing a reclassification of the connection after the handler is already created. Fix: configure ALPN before accept and propagate the result through the hand-off.

Re-using the same handler instance across sequential connections without re-initialising: if the handler clears state in its close() method but the factory returns the same object, residual state leaks between connections. Fix: always instantiate a fresh handler per connection or validate that reset() clears all per-connection state.

Permitting unlimited backlog on listen() without capacity planning: the kernel will buffer beyond the application-level connection limit, causing clients to establish connections that are immediately rejected at the application layer (visible as a spike in TIME_WAIT connections). Set listen(backlog) to match expected concurrency plus headroom.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: connection establishment vs. connection processing.
Open/closed principle: new services arrive through the factory/registry, not through edits to the accept path.
Information hiding: handlers see only the connected endpoint, never the listening one.
Dependency inversion: roles depend on abstract handler/factory and dispatcher interfaces.
best_practices: Let the acceptor/connector own establishment; hand the connected endpoint to a fresh handler instance and call its activation hook.
Use per-connection handler instances; never share mutable handler state across connections.
Drive acceptance/completion through a dispatcher (reactor/proactor) rather than one thread per connection when connection counts are high.
Bound the backlog (listen(backlog)) and the number of concurrent connections; apply admission control before accepting.
Close or recycle handlers deterministically on disconnect; avoid leaking per-connection resources.
Register services in a factory/registry keyed by service id so connection topology stays declarative.
Use SO_REUSEPORT (Linux ≥ 3.9) to allow multiple acceptor processes/threads to share a listen socket, spreading connection distribution and improving throughput under load.
Graceful shutdown: drain in-flight requests before closing the listening socket; use a shutdown flag checked by handler instances.

Always wrap TLS handshakes with a timeout: a TCP connection can be established but the TLS handshake can stall indefinitely (e.g., peer sends partial ClientHello and stalls). Use per-handshake timeouts (typically 5–10 s) to bound resource consumption under slow-peer or adversarial conditions. rustls tokio examples show timeout(5s, connector.connect(...)) as the canonical pattern.

Bound concurrent handshakes with a semaphore or weighted semaphore: allowing unlimited concurrent TLS handshakes can exhaust memory and CPU under connection storms. A semaphore permit pool (e.g., tokio::sync::Semaphore with 1024 permits) acquired before spawning each handshake task prevents overload; permits are released on task exit regardless of success or failure.

Prefer async TLS adaptor libraries (tokio-rustls, tokio-native-tls, async-native-tls) over blocking TLS on an async runtime thread: blocking TLS operations (certificate parsing, private-key operations) on a tokio worker thread blocks the entire task. Use tokio::task::spawn_blocking for blocking TLS operations, or use async-native-tls which is designed for non-blocking use.

Drive the accept loop through a readiness-based (epoll/ IOCP) dispatcher rather than a busy loop: even under high connection rates the OS will wake the acceptor only when a connection is available. EPOLLEXCLUSIVE (Linux 4.5+) prevents thundering-herd wakeups when multiple acceptors share a listen socket across processes or threads.

Issue a graceful close sequence (FIN, drain, close) rather than destroying the listener socket mid-connection: stop accepting new connections, signal existing handlers to drain, wait for handler completion, then close the listening socket. Abruptly closing the listener socket while connections are in-flight leaves clients with RST packets.

Close each connected endpoint deterministically on disconnect: handlers must close their owned connected socket on any error (read failure, write failure, protocol violation). Leaking connected sockets exhausts file descriptors and leaves connections in TIME_WAIT.

Register services in a factory/registry keyed by service id so connection topology stays declarative: the acceptor should not need to know the concrete handler type — it looks up the handler factory by service id (from SNI, ALPN, or a protocol negotiation result) and instantiates the handler through the factory interface.

Use SO_REUSEPORT (Linux ≥ 3.9) to allow multiple acceptor processes or threads to share a listen socket with independent epoll interest sets, spreading connection distribution across cores and improving throughput under multi-core load.

Design handler activation to be idempotent: if the handler is activated by both the accept-loop task and a timeout task, the second activation must be a no-op. Use an atomic "activated" flag or a once_cell guard to prevent double-initialisation.

For UDP-based protocols (QUIC, DTLS), treat the acceptor as owning the UDP socket and demultiplexing packets to connection handlers; unlike TCP there is no accept() call, so the acceptor must read datagrams and route them by connection id to the appropriate handler.
sources: Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert & Buschmann, Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects (Wiley, 2000) — Acceptor-Connector chapter.
https://www.cs.wm.edu/~dcschmidt/PDF/Acc-Con.pdf — original conference paper (Schmidt, 1995) with full participant model and ACE implementation detail.
https://www.cs.wm.edu/~dcschmidt/POSA/POSA2/ — POSA2 homepage listing all 17 patterns with links.
https://www.dre.vanderbilt.edu/~schmidt/POSA/POSA2/event-patterns.html — Vanderbilt mirror of the POSA2 event-patterns chapter.
https://www.dre.vanderbilt.edu/~schmidt/PDF/acc-con-siemens.pdf — early Siemens technical report on the pattern.
https://www.dre.vanderbilt.edu/~schmidt/PDF/EuroPLoP.pdf — EuroPLoP version with extended C++ implementation notes.
https://www.dre.vanderbilt.edu/~schmidt/PDF/ICCDS-96.pdf — ICDCS-96 conference paper with performance and concurrency analysis.
https://www.dre.vanderbilt.edu/~schmidt/patterns-ace.html — ACE patterns page with implementations and further links.

Guzman (Meta Engineering), "Deploying TLS 1.3 at scale with Fizz open source library" (2018) — Meta's production TLS 1.3 implementation in C++14 with async-by-default design and scatter/gather I/O. https://engineering.fb.com/2018/08/06/security/fizz/ — relevant to acceptor-connector because the acceptor/connector roles map directly onto the TLS handshake pipeline (accept side = server hello + cert, connect side = client hello + key share).

RFC 8446 — The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3 (Rescorla, 2023). https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8446 — the normative spec for TLS 1.3 connection establishment, covering the three-phase handshake (key exchange, server parameters, authentication) that acceptor-connector implementations must sequence correctly.

RFC 8448 — Example Handshake Traces for TLS 1.3 (Thomson, 2019). https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8448 — concrete byte-level TLS 1.3 handshakes with all intermediate values, useful for testing acceptor-connector implementations against the 1-RTT profile.

youyuanwu/quiche-h3 — HTTP/3 QUIC acceptor-connector bridge for tokio-quiche. Exposes standalone H3QuicheAcceptor/H3QuicheConnector whose accept()/connect() yield typed h3::quic::Connection; models graceful shutdown via endpoint.close() + wait_idle(). https://github.com/youyuanwu/quiche-h3 — shows acceptor-connector applied to UDP-based QUIC where the acceptor owns the listen socket and spawns per-connection workers.

async_smux — Rust async stream multiplexer with explicit Acceptor/Connector roles. MuxAcceptor receives peer-initiated streams; MuxConnector opens outgoing streams; MuxWorker drives I/O. Demonstrates the pattern applied to in-connection stream multiplexing with keep-alive timeouts and orderly shutdown. https://docs.rs/async_smux/latest/async_smux/

gel_stream — Rust network library with Acceptor and Connector types for TCP and TLS. Acceptor::new_tcp() binds and produces connections; Connector::new() dials and produces a connected stream. Supports tokio runtime natively. https://docs.rs/gel-stream/latest/gel_stream/

Boost.Asio — basic_socket_acceptor class reference (ip::tcp::acceptor). Documents synchronous accept(), async_accept(), bind(), listen(), and SO_REUSEPORT usage. The canonical C++ acceptor implementation underlying most modern C++ network frameworks. https://www.boost.org/doc/libs/master/doc/html/boost_asio/reference/ip__tcp/acceptor.html

BestHub — "Understanding Netty's Asynchronous Model, Epoll, and I/O Multiplexing" (2024). Explains Netty's bossGroup (acceptor/connector) / workerGroup (handler) split and how ServerBootstrap wires Reactor + Acceptor-Connector into a configurable pipeline. https://www.besthub.dev/articles/understanding-netty-s-asynchronous-model-epoll-and-io-multiplexing-theory-jni-integration-and-a-hand-written-epoll-server-eee2e6e874ed

Istio & Envoy Insider — "Listener connection establishment details" — describes Envoy's TcpListenerImpl onAccept path: epoll_wait → accept() → ActiveTcpSocket → ListenerFilterChain → findFilterChain → newConnection. Shows how service mesh proxies structurally implement acceptor-connector: one process owns the listen socket (Envoy worker), filter chains act as service handler factories. https://istio-insider.mygraphql.com/en/latest/ch2-envoy/arch/listener/listener-connection.html

Delarue & Fernandez — "Extension and Java Implementation of the Reactor-Acceptor-Connector Pattern Combination" (SciSpace). Adds Controlled-Reactor pattern for Java where the Initiation Dispatcher auto-tunes thread count based on performance constraints. Extends the acceptor-connector with a Performance Manager that creates/destroys Event Dispatcher threads dynamically. https://scispace.com/pdf/extension-and-java-implementation-of-the-reactor-acceptor-2groy2dhty.pdf

Chapter 7 — The ACE Acceptor-Connector Framework (O'Reilly). The definitive chapter on ACE's C++ acceptor-connector implementation with Acceptor, Connector, Service_Handler, and Acceptor_Impl template classes. https://www.oreilly.com/

Poco::Net::SocketConnector — implements the Connector role for the Poco C++ library. Registers with a SocketReactor, initiates non-blocking connect, creates ServiceHandler on completion. Documents the acceptor-connector roles in a production framework. https://docs.pocoproject.org/current/Poco.Net.SocketConnector.html

POSA2 Event Handling Patterns — canonical origin: Acceptor-Connector decouples connection and initialization from the processing that follows and can layer on Reactor. https://www.dre.vanderbilt.edu/~schmidt/POSA/POSA2/event-patterns.html
Netty ServerBootstrap API — documents separate parent (acceptor) and child EventLoopGroups and child handlers for accepted channels. https://netty.io/4.1/api/io/netty/bootstrap/ServerBootstrap.html

Java SE ServerSocketChannel API — documents OP_ACCEPT registration, non-blocking accept readiness, and the blocking mode of accepted channels. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/nio/channels/ServerSocketChannel.html

Apache Kafka SocketServer source — documents one Acceptor per listener assigning accepted connections to Processor selectors and handler threads. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/apache/kafka/trunk/core/src/main/scala/kafka/network/SocketServer.scala

Apache Kafka KIP-402 — describes connection storms, unbounded accepted-connection queues, acceptor backpressure and active-connection limits. https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/spaces/KAFKA/pages/97553944/KIP-402+Improve+fairness+in+SocketServer+processors
Linux listen(2) manual — explains pending-connection queue limits and refusal or retry behaviour when the queue is full. https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/listen.2.html

uWSGI documentation, Serializing accept() — describes thundering-herd wakeups and wasted CPU when many workers monitor one listening socket. https://uwsgi-docs-additions.readthedocs.io/en/latest/articles/SerializingAccept.html

Apache Pekko Streams TCP documentation — shows bind producing IncomingConnection values and outgoingConnection for connector-side flows. https://pekko.apache.org/docs/pekko/current/stream/stream-io.html

related_patterns_notes.reactor: a readiness demultiplexer that dispatches events; Acceptor-Connector separates accept/connect setup and handler activation, and can layer on top of it.
related_patterns_notes.proactor: a completion demultiplexer for asynchronous operations; Acceptor-Connector still separates establishment from post-connection service processing.
